group.title: Money and finance
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Money you put into something in the hope of getting more back later.
examples: Buying that small flat turned out to be a smart {investment}.
wrong: The investment lost half its value, so it made them rich.

words.meaning: A number that shows banks how likely you are to pay back money you borrow.
examples: Paying bills on time helps your {credit score}.
wrong: His credit score is high because he never pays his bills.

words.meaning: To officially borrow money from a bank that you must pay back.
examples: They had to {take out a loan} to pay for the new roof.
wrong: She took out a loan, so now the bank owes her money.

words.meaning: A bank or person that gives money which must be paid back.
examples: The {lender} agreed to give us the money at a low rate.
wrong: The lender is the person who borrows money and pays it back later.

words.meaning: A person who receives money and must pay it back later.
examples: Every {borrower} has to make a payment each month.
wrong: As a borrower, he gave money to the bank and waited for it to pay him back.

words.meaning: To pay back money that you owe.
examples: It took me five years to {repay} my student loan.
wrong: He repaid the money, so he still owes every cent.

words.meaning: An amount of money saved for the future.
examples: They built up a nice {nest egg} for their retirement.
wrong: Their nest egg is the money they spend on lunch every day.

words.meaning: An amount you are allowed to spend from your bank account beyond the money in it.
examples: I used my {overdraft} to pay the rent before payday.
wrong: Her overdraft showed that she had lots of spare money in the bank.

words.meaning: A bank account for keeping money you don’t plan to spend soon.
examples: She puts a little into her {savings account} every month.
wrong: I keep my savings account for money I spend every day on coffee.

words.meaning: Having a lot of money or valuable things.
examples: He comes from a {wealthy} family that owns three houses.
wrong: They were so wealthy that they couldn’t pay for food.

words.meaning: To receive money or property from someone after they die.
examples: She {inherited} her grandmother’s house by the sea.
wrong: He inherited the farm from his son, who is still alive and young.

words.meaning: Money or property that you receive from someone who has died.
examples: He used his {inheritance} to start a small business.
wrong: Her inheritance was the salary she earned at her new job.

words.meaning: Connected with money and how it is managed.
examples: The company is in serious {financial} trouble.
wrong: My financial advisor helps me choose the right shoes.

words.meaning: Money given by a government or organization for a special purpose.
examples: The school received new {funding} for a science lab.
wrong: The project got lots of funding, so it had no money at all.

words.meaning: The money you get from work or from an investment.
examples: His {earnings} went up after he got the promotion.
wrong: Her earnings are the bills she has to pay every month.

words.meaning: An act of buying, selling or moving money, especially through a bank.
examples: Every card {transaction} appears in the app within seconds.
wrong: The transaction never happened, because money moved between the two accounts.

words.meaning: To waste money, time or a chance in a foolish way.
examples: He {squandered} his prize money on fast cars.
wrong: She squandered her money by saving every cent carefully.

words.meaning: To let a debt or bill grow bigger and bigger.
examples: She {ran up} huge debts on her credit cards.
wrong: He ran up a big bill by paying everything off at once.

words.meaning: To have just enough money to pay for the things you need.
examples: With two jobs, they can just about {make ends meet}.
wrong: They can’t make ends meet, so they have lots of money left over each month.

words.meaning: To spend less money by being careful.
examples: We {economized} by cooking at home instead of eating out.
wrong: To economize, we bought the most expensive car in the shop.

words.meaning: Careful with money and not wasting it.
examples: My {thrifty} uncle repairs his old shoes instead of buying new ones.
wrong: She is very thrifty and spends all her pay on things she never uses.

words.meaning: Owing money because you have spent more than you have.
examples: The company has been {in the red} for three years.
wrong: We are in the red, so we have plenty of money in the bank.

words.meaning: To pay all the money you owe on a debt.
examples: They finally {paid off} their mortgage last year.
wrong: She paid off her loan, so she still owes the bank most of it.

words.meaning: The time when you stop working, usually because of age.
examples: He plans to travel a lot during his {retirement}.
wrong: In his retirement he works twelve hours a day at the office.

words.meaning: Money given by an organization for a purpose, which you don’t pay back.
examples: She got a {grant} to study music in Vienna.
wrong: He has to pay back the grant with interest, like a normal loan.

words.meaning: To pay for something, often something expensive.
examples: Who is going to {foot the bill} for the party?
wrong: His parents footed the bill, so he had to pay for everything himself.

words.meaning: A person who pays money to the government from their income.
examples: The new bridge was paid for by the {taxpayer}.
wrong: As a taxpayer, she never gives any money to the government.

words.meaning: A very large amount of money.
examples: He made a {fortune} selling his software company.
wrong: She spent a fortune on the shirt, which cost almost nothing.

words.meaning: To take an amount away from a total.
examples: The company {deducts} tax from your pay every month.
wrong: They deducted ten dollars, so my bill went up by ten dollars.

words.meaning: A form on which you tell the government how much you earned so it can work out your tax.
examples: I have to send my {tax return} before the end of April.
wrong: A tax return is a gift the government sends you on your birthday.

words.meaning: Having no extra cost added for borrowing money.
examples: The shop offers an {interest-free} payment plan for a year.
wrong: The loan was interest-free, so I had to pay ten percent extra.

words.meaning: The first part of the price you pay when you buy something expensive and pay the rest later.
examples: They saved for years to make a {down payment} on a house.
wrong: The down payment is the last amount you pay after everything else.

words.meaning: Having enough money to live comfortably.
examples: Her parents are quite {well-off} and own a holiday home.
wrong: They are well-off, so they can’t afford to buy food.

words.meaning: Having very little money for a while.
examples: I’m a bit {hard up} until I get paid next week.
wrong: He was hard up, so he bought everyone expensive gifts.

words.meaning: An amount of money paid all at once rather than in parts.
examples: When he left the company, he received a {lump sum} of ten thousand dollars.
wrong: She received the lump sum in small amounts every week for ten years.

words.meaning: To reduce the amount of money you spend on something.
examples: We need to {cut back} on takeout food this month.
wrong: We cut back on travel by taking twice as many trips.

words.meaning: The lowest amount of pay per hour that the law allows.
examples: Many young workers earn the {minimum wage}.
wrong: The minimum wage is the highest salary anyone in the country can earn.

words.meaning: The state of being legally unable to pay your debts.
examples: The shop faced {bankruptcy} after a year of poor sales.
wrong: The company’s bankruptcy came after its most successful year.

words.meaning: The amount by which a government spends more than it earns.
examples: The government plans to reduce the {budget deficit} by raising taxes.
wrong: A budget deficit means the government has a lot of extra money left over.

words.meaning: The money that ordinary people spend on goods and services.
examples: {Consumer spending} usually rises before the holidays.
wrong: Consumer spending is the money companies pay to their workers.
